nameStory: Smooth sumac gets its name from its hairless branches and leaf stems, which feel smooth to the touch. This sets it apart from its fuzzy cousin, staghorn sumac, whose velvety branches reminded early settlers of the soft antlers on young male deer.
description: Smooth sumac is a colonial shrub that forms dense thickets through underground runners, typically growing 6-15 feet tall. Its compound leaves are made up of 11-31 narrow, toothed leaflets arranged feather-like along a central stem. In summer, it produces dense clusters of tiny greenish flowers at branch tips, followed by fuzzy red berry clusters that persist through winter. The whole plant turns brilliant orange-red in fall, creating spectacular autumn displays.

idTips.label: Branches
idTips.description: Young twigs and leaf stems are completely smooth and hairless, often with a whitish or bluish waxy coating that you can rub off with your finger

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with 11-31 lance-shaped leaflets, each 2-4 inches long with sharp teeth along the edges; leaflets are smooth underneath

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dense, cone-shaped clusters of small red berries covered in fuzzy hairs that feel slightly sticky and taste tart when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies of multiple stems from underground runners, creating thickets that can cover large areas

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers packed into dense, pyramid-shaped clusters 4-8 inches long at the ends of branches in early summer

habitat: Smooth sumac thrives in sunny, well-drained locations like old fields, roadsides, forest edges, and disturbed areas throughout New England. It prefers slightly acidic to neutral soils and tolerates poor, rocky conditions where other shrubs struggle. You'll often find it colonizing slopes, abandoned lots, and areas recovering from disturbance.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late spring, unfurling from pointed buds. Look for the smooth, waxy coating on young twigs that distinguishes it from staghorn sumac.
seasonality.summer: Dense clusters of small greenish-yellow flowers appear at branch tips in June and July. The compound leaves are fully developed, showing their distinctive smooth undersides.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn spectacular shades of orange, red, and purple in early autumn. Red berry clusters ripen and become prominent as leaves drop.
seasonality.winter: Persistent red berry clusters remain visible on bare branches. Smooth, reddish-brown twigs with a whitish bloom are diagnostic even without leaves.

funFact: The fuzzy red berries are packed with vitamin C and can be soaked in cold water to make a tart, lemonade-like drink that Native Americans called 'Indian lemonade' - but never use hot water, as it will make the drink bitter!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with staghorn sumac, but smooth sumac's hairless twigs are the dead giveaway - if you can pet it without feeling fuzz, it's smooth sumac. Remember: smooth sumac = smooth stems, staghorn sumac = fuzzy like velvet.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the cashew family alongside poison ivy, smooth sumac is completely harmless to touch and actually beneficial for wildlife and erosion control. Don't confuse sumacs with poison sumac, which has white berries and grows in swamps - red berries mean safe sumac.
compareHints: Smooth sumac differs from staghorn sumac by its hairless twigs and stems, while staghorn feels velvety-fuzzy. Unlike shining sumac, smooth sumac's leaflets lack the distinctive winged margins between leaflets. Fragrant sumac has only three leaflets per leaf and a more compact growth habit, making it easily distinguished from smooth sumac's many-leafleted compound leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Staghorn sumac is easily distinguished from its relatives by its distinctively fuzzy branches - smooth sumac has smooth branches (as the name suggests), while shining sumac has a winged stem between leaflets.
Shining sumac is much smaller than staghorn sumac and lacks its fuzzy branches, while smooth sumac has completely hairless stems and duller leaves.
Fragrant sumac is much smaller and more spreading than its tall cousins like staghorn sumac, which can reach 15-25 feet.
